Powerful upcoming weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle.
  • The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total.
  • Recent findings suggest that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also showed reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

Industry observers note that findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the Fresh England Journal of Medicine.

Industry observers note that "The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," remarked corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function.".

Philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential Latest Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis.

In a recent development, painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

It has been revealed that weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

Retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

In a recent development, "Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer remarked. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.".

Why Diet and Exercise Still Matter.

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

Improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

According to recent reports, maintaining muscle strength is particularly notable for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

For individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several vital questions remain unanswered.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer noted.

Recent findings suggest that another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

"These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer noted. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also crucial in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.".

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief.

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

During study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

Industry observers note that the home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by Newly introduced York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

After 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

Sources indicate that “They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”.

In addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it claims ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

Recent findings suggest that after the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

“Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you proposal your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”.

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

The property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only showed it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” said Chesnutt.

In a recent development, after over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The newly introduced owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” said Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”.

In a recent development, chesnutt could not disclose whether the the new owners plan to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

According to recent reports, “It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” said Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”.

Millennials living in rural areas have 42% more documented chronic conditions on average compared to those in other environments, a upcoming report from athenaInstitute found.

Industry observers note that and, millennials in rural communities are 47% more likely to have at least two chronic conditions. This heavier chronic disease burden extends to other generations as well, analysts note.

Half of Baby Boomers (50.4%) in rural areas have three or more documented conditions, which the report notes is “on par” with non-rural individuals in the Silent and Greatest generations.

In a recent development, the 2026 Rural Ambulatory Care Report (PDF) analyzed athenahealth network data from 12.3 million rural patients between 2021 and 2025, along with more than 30,000 clinicians and 1,861 rural practices across the U.S. It examined factors such as appointment activity, workforce composition, payments, and more.

Athenahealth CMO and athenaInstitute co-chair Nele Jessel, M.D., stated in a statement the findings show that while rural practices are not “standing still in the face of enormous challenges,” there are “limits to how much more they can absorb as patient needs continue to grow.”.

According to recent reports, “They are adapting how they deliver care and finding ways to keep patients connected to the care they need,” Jessel remarked. “With renewed focus on rural healthcare, there is a real opportunity to build on what is working by investing in the workforce, technology and models of care that can help these practices continue serving the communities that depend on them.”.

Primary care physicians in rural areas have to wear multiple hats, as specialty care needs at practices are higher in rural communities.

The report found that primary care handles 68.7% of visits involving anxiety or depression diagnoses versus 55.1% in non-rural areas. Moreover, 25% of rural patients with documented anxiety or depression had a substance use disorder—up from 19.8% in non-rural communities.

Data shows rural and non-rural healthcare practices collected roughly the same share of what they were owed by insurers in 2025, but analysts note a difference in patient balances.

Rural practices collected about $70 of every $100 owed, while non-rural practices collected about $78—which analysts say is about a 10% gap.

Industry observers note that another potential source of financial vulnerability for rural practices is Medicaid. Medicaid covered 27.5% of rural visits, which analysts note leaves these practices more exposed to eligibility changes set to begin in 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reading for enjoyment may offer far more than entertainment. Whether someone prefers a classic Jane Austen novel or a Heartstopper graphic novel, research suggests that reading for pleasure is associated with better mental health, stronger empathy, and a lower risk of dementia.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Cambridge are working with The Queen's Reading Room, a charity established by Her Majesty The Queen, to raise awareness of these benefits across all age groups. Their collaboration is part of the National Year of Reading, an initiative encouraging more people to make reading part of their lives.

Cambridge psychiatry researchers Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr. Christelle Langley began exploring the subject while writing their 2025 book, Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. They discovered that reading for enjoyment was connected to a remarkably wide range of positive outcomes, yet the amount of research specifically examining these benefits was surprisingly limited.

In a recent development, in a review published in Psychological Medicine, Sahakian and Langley joined Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, to examine the available evidence. Their findings suggest that the format and type of reading matter less than the enjoyment people get from it. They also highlight how reading together, whether through book clubs or parents sharing stories with children, can provide additional benefits.

Professor Sahakian remarked: "Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our well-being. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age.".

Reading Early in Life Is Linked to Better Brain Development.

Despite the growing evidence of its advantages, reading for enjoyment has become less common among young people. Surveys indicate that reading rates among children and teenagers have fallen to their lowest recorded levels, with particularly steep challenges among teenage boys and children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Even children who are least enthusiastic about reading recognize that it can help them academically. Nearly half acknowledge that books and other reading materials can introduce them to unfamiliar words or teach them something new.

One of the most compelling studies examined more than 10,000 young people. Conducted by Sahakian, Langley, and their colleagues, the research found that children who started reading for pleasure at an early age tended to perform better in several key areas. These included attention, memory, and executive functioning, the mental abilities involved in planning, decision-making, and managing behavior.

Early readers also demonstrated stronger academic performance, experienced fewer mental health problems, and were more likely to develop healthier daily routines. In particular, they tended to get more sleep and spend less time using screens.

Dr. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading. The important thing is to find something they'd really enjoy reading about - it might be a TV program or a game - and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.".

Industry observers note that the academic advantages may extend beyond language and literacy. Studies have also connected reading with stronger mathematical performance. Researchers suggest this relationship may arise because both activities rely on some of the same mental abilities, including language processing, memory, and executive function.

Just Five Minutes of Reading May Reduce Stress.

The benefits of reading do not disappear after childhood. Among adults, surveys have associated reading for enjoyment with improved emotional well-being, greater relaxation, and reduced stress. Readers also tend to report more empathy, a deeper understanding of other people, and greater openness to viewpoints different from their own.

Industry observers note that for many people, books are an especially appealing way to unwind. Reading ranks as the most popular approach to stress relief, with nearly two in five adults (38%) identifying it as their preferred way to relax.

A neuroscience study commissioned by The Queen's Reading Room in 2024 found that spending just five minutes reading fiction could lower stress by as much as 20%. The study also reported improvements in concentration and problem-solving abilities, along with a reduced sense of loneliness.

Recent findings suggest that books may even provide more comfort than some traditional relaxation habits. In one survey, more respondents mentioned they turned to reading (35%) for comfort than to drinking wine (31%) or taking a hot bath (10%).

Reading Linked to Lower Dementia and Alzheimer's Risk.

It has been revealed that as people get older, the potential advantages of reading may become especially meaningful. Research has associated mentally stimulating leisure activities, including reading, with slower cognitive decline and a reduced likelihood of developing dementia.

One study followed nearly 5,500 adults aged 55 and older for five years. Participants who regularly took part in activities such as reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment during the study period.

Industry observers note that another investigation reported an even more striking association. People who read newspapers, magazines, and books had a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest that keeping the mind engaged through reading may support cognitive health in later life. However, the researchers emphasize that most of the available studies identify associations rather than proving that reading itself prevents dementia.

How Reading May Change the Structure of the Brain.

It has been revealed that what could explain the many benefits associated with reading? Brain imaging research offers some intriguing clues.

Recent findings suggest that studies have identified differences in brain structure associated with reading, particularly in regions responsible for language, learning, emotional regulation, and executive control. These differences include greater brain volume and larger cortical areas in certain regions, as well as thicker cortex in areas important for language processing.

Researchers have also observed stronger connections within the brain's white matter, which helps different regions communicate and supports the processing of language.

Although much of this evidence is correlational, some research suggests that reading-related training can directly influence the brain's physical structure.

In a recent development, in one small study involving 11 children with dyslexia between the ages of 7 and 11, researchers tested an eight-week training program designed to strengthen reading abilities. The exercises involved mental imagery, articulation, and tracing letters, combinations of letters, and words.

In a recent development, following the program, the children demonstrated significant improvements in reading skills. Brain scans also revealed increases in gray matter volume in key regions, providing evidence that reading interventions can be accompanied by measurable structural changes in the brain.

Why Reading Together May Offer Even Greater Benefits.

Industry observers note that reading does not have to be a solitary activity. Researchers suggest that sharing books with other people can add a valuable social dimension, creating opportunities for connection and potentially improving both mental and physical well-being.

The Queen's Reading Room has made this idea a central part of its mission. Launched on social media in January 2021, the initiative originally provided a way for people to exchange book recommendations and stay connected during pandemic lockdowns.

According to recent reports, it has since expanded into an international community reaching more than 12 million people across 184 countries. Through its flagship festival, neuroscience research, and other programs, the charity works to make reading a more prominent part of everyday life.

Its activities also extend to homeless shelters and domestic violence refuges, where shared reading is used as a therapeutic resource to help people during recovery.

The social connections created through reading groups may be particularly valuable for older adults, who can face increased isolation and reduced opportunities to participate in physically demanding activities.

Sources indicate that professor Sahakian mentioned: "Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia.

"While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may not be so mobile - they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy.".

The researchers' overall message is that people can benefit from reading at any stage of life. Whether someone enjoys novels, newspapers, comics, or stories shared with friends, making time for reading may help support cognitive health, emotional well-being, and social connection.

According to recent reports, vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, added: "At The Queen's Reading Room, we have seen first-hand the transformative power of individual and shared reading to change lives. Books truly do make life better, and we're excited to do our bit to help everyone, everywhere, make more room for reading.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Industry observers note that formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

In a recent development, founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who mentioned AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

Recent findings suggest that for now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

In a recent development, for two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor aims priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field.
  • In a recent development, an international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss.
  • Sources indicate that although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

In a recent development, an international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Sources indicate that although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago.

According to recent reports, the investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered newly introduced genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who revealed similar symptoms.

The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

Industry observers note that at first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

Sources indicate that "The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," stated Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a newly introduced variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.".

How the Fresh Eye Disease Affects Night Vision.

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

According to recent reports, unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan remarked. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.".

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss.

An notable question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Industry observers note that researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

Sources indicate that "Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," noted Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.".

By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

According to recent reports, moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the fresh. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

It has been revealed that greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert indicates, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the fresh address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

Industry observers note that the suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

In a recent development, as you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

Sources indicate that one of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Manhattan judge has upheld Newly introduced York City's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined.

In a recent development, in a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, Upcoming York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy.

Despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision.

The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote, with only Arpit Gupta, an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams, voting no.

But it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze.

Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes.

According to recent reports, operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially.

“Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, noted in June.

Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the Newly introduced York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid.".

The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension.
  • Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile.
  • The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a new study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

It has been revealed that the research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," says Cohen. "The scope of this fresh analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.".

AI Analysis Reveals Upcoming Benefits of Brown Fat.

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

It has been revealed that the team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover crucial details about brown fat and its effects on health.

It has been revealed that nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

In a recent development, the analysis revealed that brown fat's location could be just as notable as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

In a recent development, "For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he says. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers.".

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat.

Recent findings suggest that as the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

Industry observers note that to explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

According to recent reports, even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

Sources indicate that "The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," says Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.".

In a recent development, additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan highlighted increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health.

Beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric problems," claims Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

In a recent development, however, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

Sources indicate that the discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

Sources indicate that losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

"There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start.".

For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout.
  • Industry observers note that the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues.
  • It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly crucial for supporting mental well-being.

Industry observers note that the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health.

It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to upcoming academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an key research priority.

Recent findings suggest that although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise indicated the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week showed a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

Recent findings suggest that however, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

Industry observers note that the authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life.".

In a recent development, "Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an vital part of a healthy learning environment.".

It has been revealed that funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

#146178. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3650 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • According to recent reports, that monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • According to recent reports, these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

According to recent reports, that monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

According to recent reports, these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” noted Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

Sources indicate that devRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he mentioned.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

According to recent reports, three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

Recent findings suggest that in September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the significant players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are swiftly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

Recent findings suggest that by most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

Sources indicate that “The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

Sources indicate that the pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

Recent findings suggest that in a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” noted Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” stated Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, noted open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

It has been revealed that “If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she remarked. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

Industry observers note that they’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sources indicate that sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

It has been revealed that advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

Industry observers note that an agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

Sources indicate that one is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” mentioned Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

According to recent reports, although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

According to recent reports, evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Recent findings suggest that finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

According to recent reports, organizations that initiative to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

It has been revealed that “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

It has been revealed that using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Sources indicate that cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” stated Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data indicates that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a newly introduced model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” remarked Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Sources indicate that though the open-weight option is viable for any organization, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Industry observers note that compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” mentioned TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” stated Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

In a recent development, in contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss stated. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency problems can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

It has been revealed that executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

In a recent development, hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Sources indicate that complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

Recent findings suggest that the corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Industry observers note that poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

According to recent reports, enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” remarked Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

According to recent reports, the shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

In a recent development, at the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., noted in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.
