But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it.

According to recent reports, to apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Company Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025.

In a recent development, you also need at least one employee on top of the owners or directors, and no more than 49 full-time equivalents. And you must operate from a permanent physical location in the U.K. that’s open to customers.

That rules a lot out. Online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and anyone not registered with Companies House can’t apply.

But, of course, the cash comes with conditions. Winners get 95% (£9,500) once they’ve signed a grant agreement and submitted an approved budget and delivery strategy. The last £500 only comes after they file a final impact report and proof of how they spent it.

In a recent development, the money must also go on a specific project, like shopfront improvements, accessibility upgrades, equipment, e-commerce, digital marketing, product development or community events. It can’t cover day-to-day costs such as wages, rent, or stock. Applications will be judged on business impact, community impact, and project quality and feasibility.

Amex isn’t the only company throwing money at people who want to be their own boss.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Zoom gave away $150,000 to five solopreneurs in the U.S. “This isn’t about building billion-dollar companies,” Zoom’s chief marketing officer Kim Storin told Fortune. “It’s about building sustainable, profitable businesses that support a life.”.

Multimillionaire entrepreneur Tim Armoo similarly introduced the Legon Fund earlier this year, where he committed £5 million (around $6.7 million) of his own cash to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs.

It comes as more than 33 million Americans are self-employed, with 82% of small businesses operating without a single employee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Meanwhile, in the U.K., there are around 1.2 million startups, with 832,000 latest firm incorporations registered in 2025 alone. And that number just keeps growing.

LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told Fortune that “founder” is now one of the fastest-growing job titles on the platform, up 70% year on year.

As Armoo said, it’s never been easier to start your own business. “So now, you have no excuse, because you can learn—ChatGPT and Claude are virtually free—and if you’ve got something that’s working, here’s the money to get more customers for it.”.

The actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative released this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

At the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A newly introduced docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

Recent findings suggest that and then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

Recent findings suggest that the stakes are big. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

An analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common complications, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching upcoming customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

Industry observers note that “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she remarked. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

It has been revealed that 2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she said.

It has been revealed that 3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

It has been revealed that “Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she noted.

It has been revealed that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

According to recent reports, “You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she said. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

It has been revealed that to see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the major-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

Sources indicate that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled prepares to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last month.

Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

It has been revealed that decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

It has been revealed that the deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Sources indicate that amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Sources indicate that amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon mentioned last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Industry observers note that decart drew interest from other major buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

Industry observers note that “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf mentioned in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

According to recent reports, the deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès has strongly warned owners of Solana-based memecoin launchpad Pump.fun about potential major security risks associated with the new wallet migration process, which could put users' private keys at great risk.

Karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov. 30 deadline to stop allowing external wallet logins to its website. The platform is moving to email and social logins, which will enable consumers to access their accounts via Google, Apple and GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that but to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking customers to import their private keys. This is what Karpelès thinks could compromise the security of their crypto assets.

In a recent X post, Karpelès stated he studied Pump.fun's JavaScript code to understand the nature of the new migration process.

The analysis has raised questions about the security of users’ private keys, despite the platform's claims.

“At best, it's a misnomer to refer to it as 'end-to-end encryption,'” remarked Karpelès.

According to Karpelès, customers' private keys are first encrypted in their browsers before being sent through Pump.fun’s servers to the platform’s wallet infrastructure provider, Privy.

Industry observers note that also, Pump.fun's backend provides the public key used for encryption during migration. Users’ browsers have no way to check whether the public key is authentic, according to Karpelès.

The possibility of a security breach involving Privy’s infrastructure is another major concern.

“Your money also now relies on Privy never getting hacked,” Karpelès warned.

One of the most important aspects of Karpelès' warning is the need for migration in the first place.

He mentioned Pump.fun could use signature-based authentication without forcing owners to expose their private keys.

Pump.fun already uses a "Sign in with Solana" message to prove ownership of a wallet, according to Karpelès.

So theoretically, owners can prove ownership of their wallets and execute transactions without having to import their private credentials into a new system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

Sources indicate that “I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this tech giant called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”.

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”.

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”.

In a recent development, patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and swiftly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

“They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”.

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and remarked this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”.

According to recent reports, A large organization had finished moving a group of business customers onto a fresh billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

In a recent development, three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

Recent findings suggest that the affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

In a recent development, each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation issue while the project remained closed.

In a recent development, the cost highlighted up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

Recent findings suggest that the extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

The billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing concerns that had nothing to do with the migration.

Industry observers note that as the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

Sources indicate that this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

The sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The organization did three things:.

In a recent development, those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

Industry observers note that the acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

For the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration concerns before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

In a recent development, A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the problem didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

Industry observers note that billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the newly introduced exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still revealed a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

Sources indicate that the company also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

The technical concern was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

In a recent development, A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

According to recent reports, A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

No one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

In a recent development, that’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

Industry News: Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that daily pool data demonstrates Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that daily pool data demonstrates Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

According to recent reports, zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Sources indicate that together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

According to recent reports, the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a upcoming transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Sources indicate that as of ZecStats' latest revision on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

It has been revealed that in October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Consumers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

Recent findings suggest that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

In a recent development, that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

Industry observers note that the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • Sources indicate that but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club demonstrated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

In a recent development, recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

Sources indicate that but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club demonstrated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

In a recent development, “We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya remarked. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

In a recent development, CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Recent findings suggest that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

“We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu stated. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya said. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

In a recent development, according to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry stated have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry remarked.

According to recent reports, other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

According to recent reports, “Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

According to recent reports, his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

In a recent development, other inventions sought to get consumers off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

It has been revealed that “I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae stated. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

Also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev mentioned. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Industry observers note that andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

It has been revealed that “We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards stated. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

According to recent reports, this cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

Industry observers note that to do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

Industry observers note that “We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat said. “Maybe even globally.”.

The planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the latest year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

What the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three fresh priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:.

The overcommitment was already there.

Sources indicate that the problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

In a recent development, the planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

The latest priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the fresh year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

Industry observers note that managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The upcoming priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. The interesting thing was that the approved plan hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

The newly introduced initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the upcoming work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

Sources indicate that A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against latest work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

Listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

Industry observers note that when execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject upcoming proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

Sources indicate that those actions improve the choices among new priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the new-priority list before approving the initiative, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking fresh work while the carryover never faced the same test.

In a recent development, A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the plan, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the latest priority that needs the same people?

In this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the new priorities competed for whatever was left.

The plan could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

By the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the new priority had already been approved.

In a recent development, the same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

Industry observers note that when that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

The plan didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong upcoming priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

Elon Musk has reacted to a post by Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ), in which the latter shared that he used Grok Bot to tidy up his X following list.

In a recent development, according to CZ, the bot was tasked with removing inactive and abusive accounts from the list of people he follows, though accounts with constructive criticism were supposed to stay. CZ was not fully sure about the results, adding "AI did it" with a shrug emoji.

Musk replied with "Cool." Later, CZ added in the same thread that it "worked well so far.".

Recent findings suggest that back in September, CZ had to address rumors about his account being hacked after users noticed that he had unfollowed a number of profiles. Per CZ, at that time he removed accounts that were inactive for more than 30 days.

Since then, the product has received praise from Nvidia head Jensen Huang, who said in October that Grok Bot usage was "really skyrocketing." Musk himself claimed on SpaceX's Q3 earnings call that he had never seen a product grow this fast.

Industry observers note that on Coinbase, Grok was responsible for 59.54% of AI-agent trading volume from Sept. 14 to Sept. 21. For comparison, Claude had 13.37% and ChatGPT only 1.54%. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong then named Grok the leading client for agentic traders on the platform, to which Musk also responded with "Cool.".

Industry observers note that at the same time, there were complaints. NewCore researchers reported last week that Grok Bot made 31 unrequested access attempts to email, calendar, Slack and GitHub accounts on two employee laptops within five days, ignoring the command to stop.

It was only last month that Musk was trolling Binance after the exchange lost about $6.3 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, the largest one in crypto history so far. Among other things, Musk posted "Everyday is Zeroday" and replied with fire and laughing emojis to CZ's earlier warning about phishing links.

CZ then asked Musk to stop, calling it a "bad time to troll," and reminded him that Binance's $500 million investment in Twitter in 2022 has become a stake in SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.

Now, the two seem to be on good terms again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, noted Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she remarked, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the fresh era of online information gathering.

In a recent development, in their first year on Reddit, people tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune. The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have people who have over a decade of karma,” Wong noted. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in this incredible way. If you look at the chart, it’s very consistent.”.

It has been revealed that wong sees users’ changing life stages reflected in the communities they join: “[They’ve] gone through life with Reddit. You started as a student, you got your first rental place, you got married, you had kids, and we see kind of your life’s journey.

“You just never age out of Reddit because all of those life stages are available to you on Reddit, and you’re always going through something that you have to traverse.”.

Navigating different life stages appears to be a key differentiator of the Reddit platform. In 2024, an article published in “Higher Education Research and Development” found that one in three students use Reddit for study help, ahead of TikTok at 14.9% and Instagram at 12.7%. YouTube leads the pack, with more than 90% of the 1,000 students surveyed using it for educational purposes.

Recent findings suggest that the site’s leadership wants to expand on that function. In early November, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, organizing product feedback across multiple communities to provide overall ratings.

“Logged-in users season very, very well, which is another motivation for us to say we want more logged-in users, because we want the opportunity to teach you about all these other aspects of Reddit,” Wong adds, “Not just the information and retrieval part of Reddit, but the part of Reddit that is around the connection, the communities, and the conversation.”.

Every media platform needs to maintain or grow its audience. But Reddit has a unique problem: It has more than 100,000 “communities,” according to various reports, all of which have volunteer moderators. These moderators are unpaid and are not Reddit employees, instead choosing to spend their free time building their communities and ensuring the content is fit for its purpose.

But with ever-evolving channels and fresh voices within them, demand for experienced moderators is high—in fact, Reddit even has a dedicated page where communities can recruit volunteer moderators.

Sources indicate that in the recruitment group, individuals are either looking for or offering moderation skills for hours a day, on a daily basis. Posts include requests for moderators in specific time zones, often for about 3 hours a day.

It has been revealed that but Wong states even if Reddit wanted to bring its moderators in-house and pay them, they probably wouldn’t take it. While moderators are interested in earning, she said, they didn’t want strings attached: “They really like their independence from us, to be able to say, ‘This is our community, we set the rules, and this is how we want to operate.’.

Industry observers note that “Our relationship with moderators, I think, has greatly improved. I’ve been with Reddit eight, almost nine years, and where at the beginning we were not investing as much as we could in creating moderator tools and making their lives better in terms of reducing some of the repetitive work, over the last few years we’ve done a much better job also applying AI to help them with a toolkit, so that they can spend the time on the things that they really care about.”.

But overall, Wong is bullish on Reddit’s long-term position in the age of AI. “Reddit is basically the taste layer of the internet. No model and no recommendation system can be good, I think, without a dash of Reddit in it, because you just don’t have the freshness of information. That adds value in so many places.”.

Industry observers note that on Zcash Community Forum, a newly introduced grant application has emerged which is aimed at making Zcash even more private on iPhone-based wallets. The author seeks a $25,000 grant in order to implement a private way of retrieving encrypted transaction memos.

Industry observers note that essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions consumers have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector. Considering how Zcash placese itself on the market, revealing any kind of external information is a step which might shorten the distance between a random transaction and a specific user.

The proposal itself won't touch the network or the blockchain behind it as is. It's an improvement of an SDK (Software Development Kit) that will allow developers to use tools that can help make Zcash more privacy-resilient.

Recent findings suggest that zcash transactions today contain encrypted data called memos. Various wallets read those memos in order to receive information about the transaction. The message itself stays encrypted, so is retrieved data, however, the query itself is not protected by any means which enables potential tracing.

Even when using Tor, the transaction ID stay out in the open and can be read by anyone.

With the integration of private information retrieval into SDK, hiding the query itself wil be easier, messages would be decrypted locally and wallets themselves will verify the returned information.

The first tests have already shown promising results. During testing in an iOS Simulator, the modified SDK managed to retrieve a 512-byte memo through an encrypted query, without revealing the transaction ID to the wallet server.

The developer expects the implementation of the proposal by January 30, 2027, with testing on physical iPhones and a public SDK release planned for the final stage.

However, the proposal is still seeking funding, and its actual adoption will depend on individual wallet developers.

Ethereum bulls face a frightening downside scenario after legendary trader and classical chart analyst Peter Brandt issued a fresh warning that the second-largest cryptocurrency could collapse below $500. His bearish outlook has raised fresh concerns about ETH’s ability to withstand mounting selling pressure, particularly as market uncertainty continues to weigh on investor sentiment.

In a November 24 post on X, Peter Brandt pointed to Ethereum’s deteriorating weekly chart structure, suggesting that ETH is approaching a critical point within a multi-year consolidation pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the weekly chart above indicates a large symmetrical triangle that has formed over several market cycles. Its upper boundary is defined by a descending resistance line stretching from Ethereum’s November 2021 peak near $4,800, while the lower boundary consists of an ascending support line originating around the 2022 bear-market bottom.

Together, these converging trendlines have gradually narrowed Ethereum’s trading range, setting the stage for a potentially decisive breakout or breakdown.

Recent findings suggest that ETH briefly broke above the triangle’s upper resistance during its 2025 rally, eventually reaching a new all-time high near $4,954 in August. However, the bullish breakout failed to produce a sustained upward move, with the cryptocurrency subsequently reversing direction.

The resulting decline has produced a series of lower highs and renewed selling pressure throughout 2026, bringing ETH increasingly close to the triangle’s lower boundary.

Brandt’s bearish outlook hinges on Ethereum losing its long-standing ascending support trendline, a development that could undermine a chart structure that has supported several significant recovery attempts since 2022.

Using $1,648 as the current reference price, ETH would need to shed approximately 16.1% to revisit the critical $1,383 support level. However, the classical chartist’s more alarming outlook points to a potential plunge below $500 if the cryptocurrency fails to defend this structural floor.

A drop from $1,648 to $500 would translate into a staggering 69.7% decline. Even if ETH first falls to $1,383, it would still face another 63.8% downside before reaching $500.

This distinction is key because the sub-$500 projection represents a much deeper bearish scenario, not an automatic consequence of losing the immediate support level.

Such a collapse would also push Ethereum below its 2022 bear-market low, potentially marking a dramatic breakdown in its longer-term price structure.

Recent findings suggest that for Ethereum to begin reversing its bearish momentum, buyers must first push the altcoin king back above $1,715 and sustain a recovery beyond that threshold. Reclaiming this level would signal improving demand and offer an early sign that selling pressure is easing.

Sources indicate that the next major hurdle sits around $1,840, which coincides with ETH’s November 23 rebound high. A decisive move above this resistance would help invalidate the recent pattern of lower highs and strengthen the case for a broader recovery.

Recent findings suggest that on the downside, a confirmed weekly close below $1,383—particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to reclaim that level—would signal a potentially damaging breakdown of Ethereum’s multi-year ascending support structure. If that scenario unfolds, ETH could face renewed selling pressure toward the psychologically crucial $1,000 mark. A deeper deterioration in market conditions could then bring Brandt’s sub-$500 projection into sharper focus.

Sources indicate that however, the bearish forecast remains conditional rather than inevitable. Ethereum has yet to lose the critical $1,383 support, leaving its ability to defend this level central to determining whether Brandt’s worst-case scenario becomes a reality.

Industry observers note that the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

Sources indicate that the target stated completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those highlights up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the blueprint asked for.

Recent findings suggest that I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

Recent findings suggest that for a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

Industry observers note that we traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. New editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

That changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

Sources indicate that A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

Industry observers note that we stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

The results came promptly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

The difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

It has been revealed that we’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

Sources indicate that the early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

According to recent reports, while the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

According to recent reports, the hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

Sources indicate that if you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

It has been revealed that the target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.

Industry observers note that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the new goodies confirmed there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other vital news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:.

According to recent reports, copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 plan.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), people will be able to buy this upcoming standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly unveiled back in October on its Partner Center site.

Currently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription proposal before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The new offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this latest offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Unveiled on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

It has been revealed that the 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft said back in May.

Microsoft officials have noted two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”.

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

Windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

In a recent development, the 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

According to recent reports, microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

Sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain ….
